summary: Describes common practices for gateways that interwork between the telephone network (PSTN) and SIP networks. It sorts the uses of such gateways, gives use cases, and identifies mechanisms needed, including encapsulating PSTN signaling inside SIP and translating it into SIP. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP-T is the set of agreed ways to connect a SIP telephone network to the traditional telephone network. It works by carrying the old signalling inside the SIP message so nothing is lost, and copying the few pieces that routers need into the ordinary SIP headers.

subtitle: How a SIP telephony network talks to the traditional telephone network without losing what the phone network said.

tldr.problem: A voice-over-IP network cannot replace the telephone network on its own: calls still have to connect to it, and the telephone network carries information in its signalling that plain SIP cannot express.
tldr.mechanism: SIP-T is a set of mechanisms, not a new protocol. At the gateway the telephone signalling is carried inside the SIP message as a MIME body, and the parts needed for routing are copied into the SIP headers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3372 is BCP 63 and is not obsoleted. It frames the mechanisms and points to the documents that specify them.

today: RFC 3372 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 63, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It is a framework: the mechanisms it names are specified in the documents it references, such as RFC 3261 for SIP and RFC 3204 for the ISUP MIME type.

sections.title: Why a SIP Telephony Network Needs the PSTN
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is an application-layer control protocol that can establish, modify and terminate multimedia sessions or calls, including multimedia conferences and Internet telephony. SIP is one of the key protocols used to implement Voice over IP (VoIP). Although performing telephony call signalling and transporting the associated audio media over IP yields significant advantages over traditional telephony, a VoIP network cannot exist in isolation from traditional telephone networks, so it is vital for a SIP telephony network to interwork with the PSTN.

The popularity of gateways that interwork between the two networks motivated the publication of a set of common practices that can assure consistent behaviour across implementations. This document taxonomizes the uses of PSTN-SIP gateways, provides use cases, and identifies the mechanisms necessary for interworking.

Two characteristics matter. The first is feature transparency with respect to the PSTN: traditional telecom services such as call waiting and freephone numbers, implemented in PSTN protocols such as Signaling System No. 7 (SS7), should be offered by a SIP network in a manner that precludes any debilitating difference in user experience. The second is routability of SIP requests: a SIP request that sets up a telephone call should contain enough information in its headers to be routed to its destination by proxy servers, which most commonly entails carrying parameters of the call such as the dialed number over from SS7 signalling to SIP requests.

SIP-T provides these two characteristics through two techniques, encapsulation and translation. At a SIP-ISUP gateway, SS7 ISUP messages are encapsulated within SIP so that information necessary for services is not discarded. At the same time, some critical information is translated from the ISUP message into the corresponding SIP headers, because intermediaries such as proxy servers that make routing decisions cannot be expected to understand ISUP.

Pure SIP has all the instruments needed to establish and terminate calls, but no baseline mechanism to carry mid-call information such as the ISUP INF/INR query along the signalling path during the session. A provision to transmit such optional application-layer information is also needed. The document focuses on SS7 ISUP and specifies behaviour across ISUP-SIP interfaces only; many other signalling modes exist, such as SS7 ISUP, BTNUP, Q.931 and MF.
sections.plainLanguage: Telephone networks carry more than the number you dialled. They carry signals about call waiting, freephone service and the like, in a signalling system SIP has never heard of. SIP-T is the agreed set of ways to carry that information across, and to copy out the parts that SIP routers need.

sections.title: The Agents in a SIP-T Network
sections.content:
SIP-T is not a new protocol; it is a set of mechanisms for interfacing traditional telephone signalling with SIP, intended for use where a VoIP network interfaces with the PSTN. Using SIP-T there are three basic models for how calls interact with gateways: calls that originate in the PSTN can traverse a gateway to terminate at a SIP endpoint such as an IP phone; an IP phone can make a call that traverses a gateway to terminate in the PSTN; and an IP network using SIP may serve as a transit network between gateways, so a call may originate and terminate in the PSTN but cross a SIP-based network in the middle.

The primary agents are the PSTN, the collection of interconnected local, long-distance and international phone companies; IP endpoints, meaning any SIP user agent that can act as an originator or recipient of calls; and proxy servers, SIP intermediaries that route SIP requests to their destinations.

IP endpoints include gateways, which provide a point of conversion between signalling protocols such as ISUP and SIP as well as between circuit-switched and packet-switched audio media; the term Media Gateway Controller (MGC) is used in the examples for large-scale clusters of decomposed gateways and control logic, so a SIP-ISUP gateway speaks ISUP to the PSTN and SIP to the Internet and converts between the signalling types and interchanges the associated bearer audio media. They also include SIP phones, the end-user devices that originate or terminate SIP VoIP calls, and interface points between networks where administrative policies are enforced, which may be middleboxes, proxy servers or gateways.

The SS7 interfaces of a particular gateway determine the ISUP variants that gateway supports, and that in turn determines whether it can provide feature transparency while terminating a call.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of box appear in every SIP-T call: the old telephone network, a gateway that speaks both languages, proxy servers that route SIP requests, and the SIP phones themselves. The gateway's telephone-side interfaces decide which version of the telephone signalling it can handle.

sections.title: The Four Call Flows
sections.content:
A scenario in which a SIP network connects two segments of the PSTN is called SIP bridging. When a call destined for the SIP network originates in the PSTN, an SS7 ISUP message is received by the gateway at the point of interconnection. This gateway is, from the perspective of the SIP protocol, the user agent client for the call setup request. Traditional SIP routing is used in the IP network to determine the appropriate point of termination and to establish a SIP dialog and begin negotiation of a media session. The egress gateway then signals ISUP to the PSTN, reusing any encapsulated ISUP present in the SIP request it receives.

Preserving the received SS7 information within SIP requests at the originating gateway, and reusing it when signalling to the PSTN at the terminating gateway, ensures that no SS7 information critical to the instantiation of features is lost when SIP bridges calls between two segments of the PSTN.

The four flows are: PSTN origination and PSTN termination, where the originating gateway receives ISUP from the PSTN and preserves it in the SIP messages it sends to the terminating gateway, which extracts the ISUP content and reuses it when signalling to the PSTN; PSTN origination and IP termination, where the originating gateway preserves the ISUP information in the SIP messages it directs at the terminating SIP user agent, which has no use for the encapsulated ISUP and ignores it; IP origination and PSTN termination, where a SIP phone originates a VoIP call routed by one or more proxy servers to the terminating gateway, which converts to ISUP and directs the call to a PSTN interface based on the information in the received SIP header, with no ISUP encapsulation in the request; and IP origination and IP termination, which is a case for pure SIP, where neither encapsulation nor translation comes into play because there is no PSTN interworking.

Because proxy servers are usually responsible for routing SIP requests based on the Request-URI, the eventual endpoint at which a request terminates is generally not known to the originator. The originator does not select from the flows as a matter of configuration; each call is routed by the SIP network independently, and the network may instantiate any of the flows as its routing logic dictates.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four shapes a call can take: telephone to telephone across the SIP network, telephone to IP phone, IP phone to telephone, and IP phone to IP phone. Only the first three involve a gateway. The network decides which shape a given call takes, because the routers choose where it ends.

sections.title: Roles: Originator, Terminator, Intermediary
sections.content:
There are three sorts of elements in a SIP VoIP network that interconnects with the PSTN: the originators of SIP signalling, the terminators of SIP signalling, and the intermediaries that route SIP requests from the originator to the terminator.

The originator generates the SIP call setup requests, the INVITEs. When a call originates in the PSTN a gateway is the user agent client; otherwise some native SIP endpoint is. In the case of a call from the PSTN, the originating gateway preserves the ISUP information by encapsulating it in the SIP request, identifies the version of ISUP it received and provides that information in the encapsulated ISUP, usually by adding a multipart MIME body with appropriate MIME headers. It then formulates the headers of the INVITE from the parameters of the ISUP, which might for instance mean setting the To header field to the reflected dialed number of the received IAM. In the case of a SIP phone as originator there is no ISUP to encapsulate, and it would be foolhardy to require that all SIP user agents have the capability to generate ISUP, so it is not the responsibility of an IP endpoint such as a SIP phone to generate encapsulated ISUP.

The terminator is a consumer of the SIP calls, a standard SIP user agent that is either a gateway that interworks with the PSTN or a SIP phone. For a PSTN termination the egress gateway generates the ISUP appropriate for signalling to the PSTN, taking values for certain parameters from the SIP headers or extracting them directly from an encapsulated ISUP body. Generally a gateway uses any encapsulated ISUP as a template for the message it will send, overwriting parameter values as it translates SIP headers or adds values that reflect its local policies. For an IP termination the SIP user agent that receives messages with encapsulated ISUP typically disregards the ISUP message, which introduces a requirement that devices like SIP phones handle multipart MIME messages and unknown MIME types gracefully.

An intermediary such as a proxy server makes a forwarding decision for a SIP request based on values of various headers, or routable elements, including the Request-URI and route headers. Because feature transparency of ISUP is central to SIP-T, and compatibility between the ISUP variants of the originating and terminating PSTN interfaces leads to feature transparency, proxy servers might take an interest in the variants of ISUP that are encapsulated with requests: the variant itself could become a routable element. The termination of a call at a point closer to the final destination is also an important consideration, and the preference of one over the other is a trade-off between simplicity of operation and cost. Two practices are set out: converting between ISUP variants where needed, performed as close as possible to the terminating gateway, which is contingent on the availability of resources and increases call setup time; or sacrificing ISUP transparency by handing the call to a gateway that does not support the version of the originating ISUP, in which case the terminating gateway ignores the encapsulated ISUP and uses the SIP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box in the call has a job. The starting point writes the call request and hides the telephone signalling inside it. The ending point takes the signalling back out and reuses it. The servers in between only read the ordinary SIP headers, so anything they need to know must be in those headers, and they may have to choose which gateway to send the call to.

sections.title: How SIP-T Carries Telephone Signalling
sections.content:
SIP-T uses the methods and procedures of SIP as defined by RFC 3261. Encapsulation of the PSTN signalling is one of the major requirements of SIP-T: SIP-T uses multipart MIME bodies to enable SIP messages to contain multiple payloads, such as Session Description Protocol (SDP) or ISUP. Numerous ISUP variants exist today, and the ISUP MIME type enables recipients to recognise the ISUP type, and thus determine whether they support the variant, in the most expeditious possible manner.

Translation encompasses all aspects of signalling protocol conversion between SIP and ISUP, and has two components. ISUP to SIP message mapping describes the mapping at the message level: in SIP-T deployments gateways are entrusted with generating a specific ISUP message for each SIP message received and vice versa, so the rules that govern the mapping must be specified, for example that an IAM must be sent on receipt of an INVITE, and a REL for BYE. ISUP parameter to SIP header mapping describes the translation of information from ISUP to SIP, for example that the Called Party Number in an ISUP IAM must be mapped onto the SIP To header field and the Request-URI. This becomes more complicated because the headers of a SIP request, especially an INVITE, may be transformed by intermediaries, so the SIP headers and encapsulated ISUP bodies come to express conflicting values, and part of the encapsulated ISUP may be rendered irrelevant and obsolete.

Pure SIP has no provision for carrying mid-call control information generated during a session, and the INFO method should be used for this purpose. INFO is not suitable for managing overlap dialing, and its use for signalling mid-call DTMF signals is not recommended; RFC 2833 gives a recommended mechanism for that.
sections.plainLanguage: The signalling is carried as a second part of the SIP message body, beside the usual session description, with a label saying what it is. Two things happen at the gateway: it copies what the routers need into the SIP headers, and it converts whole messages, so that an INVITE becomes an initial address message and a BYE becomes a release.

sections.title: SIP Content Negotiation
sections.content:
The originator of a SIP-T request might package both SDP and ISUP elements into the same SIP message by using the MIME multipart format. Traditionally, if the terminating device does not support a multipart payload or the ISUP MIME type, it would reject the SIP request with a 415 Unsupported Media Type, specifying the media types it supports, by default application/SDP. The originator would then have to resend the request after stripping out the ISUP payload, which is a cumbersome flow.

It is therefore highly desirable to have a mechanism by which the originator can signify which bodies are required and which are optional, so that the terminator can silently discard optional bodies it does not understand, allowing a SIP phone to ignore an ISUP payload when processing ISUP is not critical. This depends on the terminator supporting a Content-type of multipart/mixed and having access to the Content-Disposition header to express criticality.

The document then shows three cases. Support for ISUP is optional, in which case the user agent accepts the INVITE irrespective of whether it can process the ISUP. Support for ISUP is preferred, in which case a user agent that does not support ISUP rejects the INVITE with a 415, and the originator strips off the ISUP and resends the INVITE with SDP only, which is then accepted. And support for ISUP is mandatory for call establishment, in which case a user agent that does not support ISUP rejects the INVITE with a 415 and the originator directs its request to a third user agent that does support it. The exchanges shown are not complete; only the messages relevant to the discussion are shown.
sections.plainLanguage: If a phone cannot handle the telephone signalling inside the request, the usual result is that it rejects the whole call and the caller has to try again without it. The document shows how the sender can mark that part as optional, so a phone that does not need it simply ignores it and the call goes through the first time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SIP-T can be employed as an interdomain signalling mechanism that may be subject to pre-existing trust relationships between administrative domains. In many legal environments, distribution of ISUP is restricted to licensed carriers, and SIP-T introduces challenges in so far as it bridges carrier signalling with end-user signalling. Any administrative domain implementing SIP-T should have an adequate security apparatus in place, including elements that manage policies for fraud and billing in an interdomain environment, to ensure that the transmission of ISUP information does not result in any security violations.

Transporting ISUP in SIP bodies may provide opportunities for abuse, fraud and privacy concerns, especially when SIP-T requests can be generated, inspected or modified by arbitrary SIP endpoints. ISUP MIME bodies should be secured, preferably with S/MIME, to alleviate this concern. The authentication properties provided by S/MIME would allow the recipient of a SIP-T message to ensure that the ISUP MIME body was generated by an authorized entity, and encryption would ensure that only carriers possessing a particular decryption key are capable of inspecting encapsulated ISUP MIME bodies in a SIP request.

SIP-T endpoints must support S/MIME signatures (CMS SignedData), and should support encryption (CMS EnvelopedData). The document introduces no new considerations for IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the telephone signalling travels inside ordinary SIP requests, any SIP endpoint could read or change it. The requirement is therefore that the signalling body be signed, so the receiver knows who produced it, and that encryption be supported, so that only the carriers entitled to it can read it.
